concept: Sequential net-edge monitoring with anytime-valid evidence

claims.text: Historical accumulated evidence is not a certificate of present profitability after edge decay. Promote warns against deleting old factors or freely resetting evidence; its proposed expiring authorization uses fresh post-restart data and separately funded revalidation epochs. Expiry and renewal are deployment rules, not a theorem that regimes persist. (low confidence)

A historical promotion certificate is not a current-edge or future-profitability certificate. In Promote, an edge that was positive and later decays falls outside the uniformly nonpositive null, and old accumulated evidence does not establish that the edge remains positive today. (low confidence)

Deleting old factors to form a rolling evidence product generally invalidates Promote’s original e-process guarantee. The authors require a separately funded test or valid mixture for restarts, including a fresh current-regime check. (low confidence)

Clipping a cost-adjusted return changes the estimand: Promote certifies the conditional mean of the bounded score, not the unbounded mean net return. Its authors warn that clipping can suppress rare economic losses and retain unclipped returns separately. A positive score certificate therefore cannot be treated as a certificate of positive raw-return expectancy. (low confidence)

Distinguish finite-sample confidence sequences from asymptotic confidence sequences. Waudby-Smith and coauthors explicitly trade nonasymptotic validity for broader CLT-like applicability; Howard and coauthors give nonasymptotic coverage under their specified conditions. An asymptotic monitoring boundary must not be reported as a finite-sample error guarantee. (medium confidence)

In Promote, changing the executable candidate definition creates a new candidate, evidence starts strictly after registration, and pre-birth observations may guide the rule but cannot enter its evidence product. These are protocol conditions for the claimed error control. (low confidence)

Promote’s authors explicitly limit their empirical audit: its sign-resampled null removes serial sign dependence, its adaptive mean-zero simulation is not a market model, and its replay omits financing, borrow fees, bid–ask dynamics, impact, taxes and capacity. The paper does not establish a profitable crypto-perpetual deployment. (low confidence)

Repeatedly inspecting ordinary fixed-sample tests can inflate false positives; a monitoring dashboard must use a sequentially valid procedure rather than repeatedly applying an ordinary terminal test. (high confidence)

Specify the sequential estimand explicitly under nonstationarity. Mineiro constructs a lower confidence sequence for the running average conditional expectation under nonnegative observations with bounded mean. That target differs from the latest conditional mean; Promote separately cautions that accumulated evidence need not certify today’s edge. Applying either construction to signed leveraged returns requires verifying its own support and moment assumptions. (medium confidence)

For dependent or changing observations, an appropriate confidence sequence can target the running average of conditional expectations rather than a stationary unconditional mean. Howard et al. explicitly allow dependence and changing means, subject to the construction’s tail or supermartingale conditions; this is not assumption-free validity for arbitrary returns. (medium confidence)

A confidence sequence provides coverage simultaneously over time and permits data-dependent stopping under its stated assumptions. Repeatedly applying a conventional fixed-sample test does not preserve its original false-positive guarantee. (high confidence)

In the Promote financial-research protocol, freeze the executable candidate, predictable scale, transaction-cost convention, bet mixture and testing allocation before scored outcomes. Accumulate evidence only after candidate birth, and begin economic exposure after the crossing observation. This is a protocol proposal, not evidence of profitable crypto trading. (low confidence)

Promote tests whether the conditional mean of its bounded net score is nonpositive at every scored post-birth date. Its dependence allowance comes from predictable betting and the conditional supermartingale argument; a zero unconditional full-sample mean alone is not the stated null. (low confidence)

Anytime validity for one candidate does not itself pay for an expanding strategy search. Promote assigns predictable lifetime testing masses whose total is at most one and uses allocation-adjusted crossing boundaries to control any false promotion, allowing dependent candidates and adaptive births. Abandoning a candidate does not replenish that budget. (low confidence)

Anytime-valid evidence has a power cost. Howard and coauthors explain that flexible stopping requires wider intervals than methods with stronger assumptions; Promote likewise notes that smaller candidate allocations require more observations to reach promotion. A valid gate may remain inconclusive for weak net effects. (medium confidence)

The ConfSeq repository documents implementations of uniform boundaries, confidence sequences and always-valid p-values. It provides a concrete implementation reference for sequential inference, but this repository description supplies no crypto-specific calibration or validation. (low confidence)

Netflix describes anytime-valid confidence bands in automated software canary tests, including a stop rule based on excluding zero and simultaneous control across quantiles and sample sizes. This is an engineering example of repeated-look inference; its experiment setting does not validate that procedure for dependent trading returns. (low confidence)

Heavy-tail robustness does not remove conditional-model assumptions. Wang and Ramdas’s baseline Catoni construction assumes a constant conditional mean and a known upper bound on conditional variance. Mineiro’s changing-mean alternative instead targets a running average and imposes nonnegative observations with bounded mean. Choose a construction only after matching the trading-score assumptions and target. (medium confidence)

The Promote preprint constructs statistical wealth by multiplying nonnegative factors based on bounded, cost-adjusted scores and bets selected from prior information. Its null requires nonpositive conditional score means on every scored date after registration; under those conditions the product is a nonnegative supermartingale with an anytime crossing bound. (low confidence)

Mineiro’s heavy-tail construction gives a lower confidence sequence for a running average conditional expectation under nonnegative observations and a bounded conditional mean, with moment conditions governing shrinking slack. Its scope does not justify applying that particular construction directly to signed trading returns without establishing a valid transformation or different assumptions. (low confidence)

The comparecast repository implements confidence sequences for time-varying average forecast-score differences and e-processes for the null that one forecaster scores no better than another on average. Its documented target is forecast scores; this repository evidence alone does not establish a test of executable net trading returns. (low confidence)

Howard et al. state that arbitrary-stopping and nonasymptotic flexibility comes at the cost of wider intervals than methods that rely on asymptotics or stronger assumptions, such as a known stopping rule. Anytime-valid monitoring therefore has an inferential precision cost. (low confidence)
